The Napoleonic Wars. A series of military conflicts waged by France under Napoleon Bonaparte against various European coalitions seeking to contain French revolutionary and imperial expansion, lasting from 1803 to 1815. The wars reshaped the political map of Europe, temporarily unified vast territories under French hegemony, and ultimately triggered a conservative reaction that established the foundations of the European state system lasting until World War One.

Napoleon, rising to power during the chaos of the French Revolution, transformed France's revolutionary cause into imperial ambition. He fought to export revolutionary ideals and French dominance while consolidating personal power. He declared himself Emperor in 1804. The Continental System was Napoleon's economic blockade of Britain, intended to strangle the British economy and isolate it from European trade. This policy both prolonged the conflict and drove Britain to support anti-French coalitions.

In 1812, Napoleon's Grand Army invaded Russia with over 600,000 troops, seeking to break Russian resistance. The Russian winter and scorched-earth tactics destroyed the Grande Armée, killing hundreds of thousands and shattering the myth of French military invincibility. The Wars of the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh Coalitions pitted European monarchies—Britain, Austria, Prussia, Russia—against France in successive waves. Each coalition broke apart until the final coalitions overwhelming French resources.

Lord Nelson's victory at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 secured British naval supremacy for over a century, preventing French invasion and forcing Napoleon to pursue continental dominance instead. Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in June 1815, where British, Prussian, and Dutch forces under Wellington and Blücher routed the French, ended his Hundred Days after escape from exile and concluded the Wars. His abdication and exile to Saint Helena closed the revolutionary era in Europe.
